title: How to finish the back of a cross-stitch piece
subtitle: Keeping thread ends secure and the reverse side neat
excerpt: The back of a cross-stitch piece does not need to look identical to the front, but it should have no long thread floats crossing more than a few squares, no loose ends that could pull through to the front over time, and no knots that create bumps visible from the face. A tidy back also makes the piece easier to frame and preserve.
sourceNotes: Cross-stitch back management technique. Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s), Internet Archive. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.
A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.

content.text: A tidy back on a cross-stitch piece comes from two habits: ending each thread correctly when finishing a colour, and not carrying the

long distances across the back to the next area of the same colour. A well-finished back has short thread ends woven under existing stitches and no long floats crossing more than three or four squares.
To end a thread, pass the needle under four or five thread runs on the back of the
in the same colour area. Pass under the runs in a zigzag direction rather than a straight line; the zigzag makes the end more secure. Pull the thread snug but not tight, then trim the tail close.

Start a new thread by weaving it under existing thread runs on the back in the colour area before beginning the first stitch. Leave a 1 cm tail and weave it in as the first few stitches are worked. Never knot the starting end; a knot creates a bump visible from the front of lightly-stitched areas.

When moving between two areas of the same colour that are more than 3-4 squares apart, end the thread in the first area and start fresh in the second. Carrying the thread across a gap creates a float that shows through light-coloured Aida from the front.

Check the back of the piece at the end of each session. Trim any thread tails that are longer than 1 cm. A tail that is left long can pull through the Aida holes to the front if the piece is handled a lot.

items.symptom: Thread ends keep coming loose and pulling through to the front
items.cause: Ends were trimmed too short or were not woven under enough thread runs.
items.fix: Weave the end under at least five thread runs in a zigzag direction. Leave 5-7 mm of tail after the last weave, not less. A tail that is too short has nothing to anchor it.

items.symptom: Dark thread floats are visible through pale Aida from the front
items.cause: Long thread carries across the back are showing through the fabric.
items.fix: Unpick the float and end the thread at the first colour area, then start a new length at the second. For pale fabrics, keep all thread carries to three squares or fewer.

content.text: A piece with a clean back is much easier to mount and frame than one with loose threads. The framer does not have to unpick anything, and the piece sits flat under the mount glass. Building the habit of tidy back-management from the first project means it never becomes a problem that needs correcting.
